prompt.context:
You are on a project to study the economics of the electricity market in a hypothetical country called Riveria. The market has three types of electricity plants: coal fired, oil fired, and gas fired. The table below summarizes the economics of each type:

Coal: Cost per unit = 35, Price per unit = 50, Annual market supply available = 10 units
Oil: Cost per unit = 75, Price per unit = 100, Annual market supply available = 15 units
Gas: Cost per unit = 125, Price per unit = 175, Annual market supply available = 25 units

The market operates on a 'Marginal Price' basis – that is, the price of all units sold will be equal to the price of the last unit sold. For example, if the market demand equals 50 units then the price of all 50 units sold will be $175 per unit irrespective of whether it is coal fired, oil fired or gas fired.
prompt.question: Answer the following questions: (1) Draw a supply/demand curve for a demand range of 0 to 50 units. (2) Who makes the most profits ($) when the market demand is 35 units? (3) Assuming no further capacity addition, within what demand ranges does each plant type make more $ profits than the others? (4) What are the implications of this kind of market conditions for your client who is in this market?

framework: Understand the marginal pricing mechanism: the price of ALL units sold equals the price of the last (most expensive) unit dispatched
Map supply stack: coal is cheapest (dispatched first, up to 10 units), then oil (units 11–25), then gas (units 26–50)
Price break points: demand 1–10 → $50 (coal price); demand 11–25 → $100 (oil price); demand 26–50 → $175 (gas price)
Calculate profits for each plant type at each price regime: Profit = (Market price − Cost per unit) × units sold
Identify which plant earns the most $ profit in each demand band
Draw strategic implications for capacity mix and competitive entry

questions.prompt: Draw a supply/demand (step) curve for a demand range of 0 to 50 units.
questions.guidance: The candidate should recognize this is a step-function supply curve, not a smooth curve. Price stays flat at $50 for demand 0–10 (only coal dispatched), jumps to $100 for demand 11–25 (oil now on the margin), and jumps to $175 for demand 26–50 (gas now on the margin). A strong answer labels each step with the fuel type setting the marginal price.

math.setup: Supply stack (cheapest to most expensive): Coal 0–10 units at $50; Oil 10–25 units at $100; Gas 25–50 units at $175
steps: Demand 0–10: only coal plants run → market price = $50
Demand 11–25: coal + oil run → market price = $100 (oil sets the margin)
Demand 26–50: coal + oil + gas run → market price = $175 (gas sets the margin)
math.answer: Step curve: flat at $50 from 0 to 10 units, step up to $100 from 10 to 25 units, step up to $175 from 25 to 50 units

questions.prompt: Who makes the most profits ($) when market demand is 35 units?
questions.guidance: At demand = 35 units, gas is on the margin, so the market price is $175 for all units. The candidate should multiply (market price − cost) × units sold for each plant type and compare totals. Oil earns the highest dollar profit.

math.setup: Market price at demand = 35 units → $175 (gas sets the margin). Profits = (175 − cost) × capacity sold
steps: Gas: (175 − 125) × 10 = 50 × 10 = $500 (only 10 of 25 gas units are needed to meet demand of 35: 10 coal + 15 oil + 10 gas = 35)
math.answer: Oil fired plants make the most profit at $1,500. Coal earns $1,400; Gas earns $500.

questions.prompt: Assuming no further capacity addition, within what demand ranges does each plant type make the most $ profits?
questions.guidance: The candidate should evaluate profit at key demand breakpoints (10, 25, 50) to determine which plant type wins in each regime. A strong answer identifies that gas plants are never the most profitable in the 0–50 demand range.

math.setup: Compare profits at demand = 10, 25, and 50 to identify crossover points
steps: Demand = 10 (market price = $50): Coal = (50−35)×10=$150; Oil = 0 (not dispatched); Gas = 0 (not dispatched) → Coal wins
Demand = 25 (market price = $100): Coal = (100−35)×10=$650; Oil = (100−75)×15=$375; Gas = 0 → Coal wins
Demand = 26 (price jumps to $175): Coal = (175−35)×10=$1,400; Oil = (175−75)×15=$1,500; Gas = small → Oil overtakes Coal
Gas is never the highest-profit plant in any demand scenario from 1 to 50
math.answer: Coal is most profitable for demand 1–25. Oil is most profitable for demand 26–50. Gas is never the most profitable plant type in this demand range.

questions.prompt: What are the implications of this market structure for your client?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate moves from quantitative analysis to strategic insight. Key themes: competitive entry risk, demand forecasting importance, portfolio diversification.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the strategic implications of the Riveria marginal-pricing electricity market for your client?

categories.name: Competitive entry risk
ideas: A new competitor entering with additional coal or gas capacity could shift the supply stack and depress market prices
Excess capacity in any plant type compresses profits for all existing players at that margin

categories.name: Demand forecasting
ideas: Accurate demand forecasting is critical because a small shift in demand can move the marginal price to a different price tier (e.g., from $100 to $175)
Over-investing in gas capacity is dangerous if demand remains below 25 units

categories.name: Portfolio diversification
ideas: Owning a mix of coal, oil, and gas plants provides stable profits across a wider range of demand scenarios
Coal provides steady low-cost profit even at low demand; oil provides the highest dollar profits at moderate-to-high demand

categories.name: Capacity strategy
ideas: Avoid over-building high-cost (gas) capacity — it earns lowest profits and only sets the market price when demand is highest
Consider strategic capacity withheld to keep prices elevated (supply-side market power)

categories.name: Regulatory/market risk
ideas: Marginal pricing regimes are subject to regulatory change; client should monitor policy developments
Entry of renewables (zero marginal cost) would collapse the price stack and destroy incumbent economics

recommendation: Client should maintain a diversified portfolio across coal and oil plant types to capture profits across the full demand range (1–50 units)
Invest in rigorous demand forecasting to anticipate which price tier the market will operate in and optimize capacity accordingly
risks: A new entrant adding oil or coal capacity would intensify competition and compress profits in the most lucrative demand bands
Demand falling persistently below 25 units would make oil and gas capacity unprofitable
next_steps: Model competitor capacity addition scenarios to stress-test the client's profit outlook
Evaluate whether acquiring or building coal capacity (lowest cost, always dispatched) provides a more defensible profit base
Conduct sensitivity analysis on demand forecasts to identify the probability-weighted optimal capacity mix
